sn44.10:1.3: For “does the self survive” (_atthattā_, resolving to _atthi attā_), compare “my self survives” (_atthi me attā_, [mn2:8.2]()) and “do gods survive” (_atthi devā_, [mn90:13.2]()). In each case the question is whether the self continues to exist (_atthi_) or not (_natthi_) after death. We find a similar usage in Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.20, where Naciketa wonders what happens to a man after he dies, as “some say he survives, while others say he does not survive” (_astīty eke nāyam astīti caike_).
sn44.10:1.7: Compare the behavior of Mogharāja at [snp5.16](). He has asked his question twice, but the Buddha was silent. Patiently, he asks a third time, and is answered at last. We have seen ample evidence of Vacchagotta’s relentless questioning. Here it is not the Buddha who loses patience, but Vacchagotta, who is so used to getting the answers he wants. It seems he is at some sort of crisis point.
sn44.10:2.3: Things that _atthi_ (“exist”, here to “continue to exist” or “survive”) were truly real and hence immortal. Thus “existence” or “survival” of the self implies eternalism. See [sn12.15:2.1]() and note.
sn44.10:2.4: That is to say, there is currently a self that will cease to exist.
sn44.10:2.5: Both BB and Ṭhānissaro translate uppadaya here as “the arising of”. However, by far the most common use of uppadaya is in the formula for the four right efforts, where, as here, it answers to the genitive of a kusala dhamma. Thus i take it in the sense of “gives rise to”. In addition, usually anuloma has a stronger meaning than “in line with” and has more a sense of “reinforces, supports”. The point then is not that the false view contradicts the Buddha’s insight (although it obviously does) but that it doesn’t help Vacchagotta.
